title: Indian Co-Owner of Sri Lanka's Jaffna Kings Arrested for Match-Fixing on Opening Day of Lanka Premier League
excerpt: The arrest by Sri Lanka's Sports Police Investigation Unit cast a shadow over the 2026 LPL launch, extending a troubled pattern for the league's most successful franchise.
body:
A co-owner of the Jaffna Kings — the most successful franchise in Lanka Premier League history with four titles — was arrested by Sri Lanka's police on Friday, just hours before the 2026 season was set to begin, casting a shadow over the tournament's opening day.

## The Arrest

The Sri Lanka Police Special Investigation Unit for the Prevention of Offences Relating to Sports took the Jaffna Kings co-owner into custody as part of an ongoing investigation into alleged sports corruption and match-fixing. The arrest came on Friday morning, July 17, mere hours before the 2026 LPL was to officially launch with an opening ceremony at the Sinhalese Sports Club Cricket Ground in Colombo.

The opening match — featuring Jaffna Kings against Galle Gallants — was still scheduled to proceed despite the arrest. Authorities have not publicly disclosed the co-owner's name, stating that investigations are continuing.

## A Troubled History

For the Jaffna franchise, this is the latest in a string of off-field controversies that have dogged an otherwise dominant team.

The franchise's predecessor, Jaffna Stallions, was abruptly removed from the league in 2021 following ownership and payment disputes. The team returned under the Jaffna Kings banner with new investors and went on to win LPL titles in 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2024 — four championships in five years.

In 2022, the franchise surfaced during a separate match-fixing investigation after a player reportedly informed authorities about an approach to manipulate matches, although no wrongdoing was proven against the team itself. The franchise underwent yet another ownership overhaul in 2025 after Sri Lanka Cricket terminated its agreement with the then-owners over alleged contractual issues.

## Sri Lanka's Tough Anti-Corruption Laws

Sri Lanka has some of the strictest anti-corruption laws in international cricket. The Prevention of Offences Relating to Sports Act, enacted in 2019, makes Sri Lanka the first South Asian nation to criminalize match-fixing. Anyone found guilty faces prison sentences of up to 10 years alongside substantial financial penalties.

This is not the first high-profile arrest under the legislation. In a separate case, Tamim Rahman — a Bangladesh-born British national who owned the LPL's Dambulla Thunders — was convicted of match-fixing and handed a four-year suspended sentence and a 24 million rupee fine by a Colombo High Court.

## Impact on the League

The 2026 LPL features five franchises competing in a double round-robin league phase followed by playoffs, with the final scheduled for August 8. Despite the arrest, the tournament is expected to proceed.

For Indian cricket fans, the case highlights the cross-border nature of franchise cricket ownership in South Asia and the growing scrutiny of integrity in T20 leagues worldwide.
